About This Edition

This edition is written for students who already know how to read short, simple words and are ready to master advanced spelling patterns. The beginning-reader phonics primer (letter sounds, blending, sight words) has been removed, since it is not needed at this level.

Every lesson follows the same 7-stage sequence, and every stage has its own fixed color and icon so you always know exactly where you are. Stages 1 and 2 (Word List and Word Sort) share a single combined page.

🗂 2. Word Sort

🗣 4. Reading Fluency
✏ 5. Proofreading

How to Use This Book

Every lesson set covers 7 stages. Stages 1 and 2 (Word List and Word Sort) share one combined page; Stages 3–7 each get their own page. A colored badge, an icon, and a 7-dot progress bar appear at the top of every page so you always know which stage you're on.

The Queen’s Terrace

The queen stepped onto the stone terrace outside the palace, a gold necklace shining at her throat. Below, smoke rose from an old furnace that had once been a menace to the whole town. She gave a small grimace at the smell, then turned back toward the cool marble surface of the steps. Deep in the cellar, the pomace left from pressing grapes still covered every surface she touched. Even so, she found solace in knowing the whole populace would soon taste the wine. The preface of her grandmother's old cookbook, its cover as tough as a turtle's carapace, still described the little pinnace that once carried barrels down the river.

The Village Rebuilds

The small village had survived a long sea voyage worth of stories. When the storm caused damage to the old cottage by the shore, the villagers found the courage to rebuild it together. They sent a message to the next town asking for extra storage space for their supplies. Before they could leave, someone had to manage the pile of baggage stacked by the door, and wrap a fresh bandage around the dog's paw. The average family might have called it too much work, but they refused to treat the old cottage like garbage. Instead, they let a hostage of cabbage leaves sit in a box marked for postage, ready to forage for more supplies at the next village package drop.

The Pirate’s Map

The old pirate map showed an island with a mild climate and an intricate network of caves. It took a delicate touch to follow the accurate directions without tearing the fragile paper. Anyone fortunate enough to find the treasure would need to be an advocate for sharing it fairly. A private letter from the senate arrived that morning, written in literate, careful hand. It described the ultimate plan: a delegate would travel to a place with a temperate climate, taste the local chocolate, and report back on the strange, spicy palate of the region. It felt like a desperate request for such a moderate reward, but the immediate answer from the crew was yes.

The Humble Climber

It seemed like a terrible idea to scramble up the wet rocks, but the climber didn't tremble. She kept her grip stable and moved with sensible, careful steps. At the top, she gave a humble nod, as if the climb had been nothing special at all. Grandpa kept an old wooden table covered in a bubble of dust near the marble fireplace. He would scribble notes on pebble-sized scraps of paper, warning that it was possible the old floor might rumble and crumble if too many people stood there at once. It sounded horrible, but he kept a small tin thimble nearby anyway, just in case anyone needed to sew the rug back together, calm and noble as ever, refusing to tumble into panic.

The Novice Cook

It took a little practice before the novice cook could slice an onion without tears. Her grandmother's best advice was simple: use plenty of spice, and never sacrifice flavor for speed. A small notice pinned above the stove reminded everyone in the office kitchen that fair justice meant sharing the last bowl of rice evenly, no matter how nice the smell of the leftover ice cream in the freezer was. Later, someone brought a steaming bowl of rice to the table, along with a bit of extra spice for flavor. It was a nice way to end a long day, though nobody wanted to roll the dice for who did the dishes. A family of tiny mice had already snuck in for the crumbs, and someone had to entice the cat out from under the table with the advice that dinner was almost ready.
